    Personal Guidance
    Even Kṛṣṇa's deepest play yields to the call of duty — let elders' summons interrupt your absorption, and serve at the right time.
    Practical Applications
    • When an elder or parent calls you mid-task today, drop your absorption immediately and respond — treat it as Yaśodā's call through Rohiṇī.
    • Notice one engagement (work, scrolling, conversation) you treat as too important to interrupt, and practice yielding it to a household duty before sundown.
    • Eat your meals at the time set by those who care for you, not by your own convenience — receive prasāda-discipline as seva, not interruption.
    Analogy

    A boy at play sees his mother appear at the riverbank and the game pauses, the toys are set down — duty's call, when carried by one who loves, has the power to interrupt even Kṛṣṇa's own absorption. The river runs on; the boys go home.

    Stories
    Rohiṇī as proxy-mother

    Rohiṇī raised Balarāma alongside Yaśodā's Kṛṣṇa in Nanda's house, a co-mother whose vātsalya for both boys is celebrated throughout the Tenth Canto. Her calling them at the riverside is the ordinary domestic act in which a great rasa hides: she calls; the universe's Lord must be coaxed.

    The Gauḍīya commentators note Rohiṇī's discernment in verse 13 — when her own call fails, she sends Yaśodā, recognizing that love-power, not authority-power, is what moves Kṛṣṇa. Her instruction in vātsalya is itself a teaching for the reader.

    Important Words
    • na upeyātām — would not return home
      Optative dual negative — They two (Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma) would not come. The grammatical emphasis matters: even svayaṁ-bhagavān, in His Vraja mode, exhibits the dual-soul fraternal play. Gauḍīya theology: Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma are tattvāntara-aikya — one in tattva though two in form.
    • āhūtau — called
      Past passive participle, dual — 'the two (when) called.' Even Bhagavān can be called — and can decline to answer. The verb itself encodes the bhakta-vaśya principle: He is responsive, not automatic.
    • krīḍā - saṅgena — because of attachment to playing
      Saṅga in Gauḍīya usage usually means devotee-association (sat-saṅga). Here it is play-attachment — but the principle is the same: attachment binds. Kṛṣṇa's krīḍā-saṅga is a willing bondage to the pleasure of His Vraja-līlā, dramatizing how His devotees are bound by His name and form.
    • putra - vatsalām — very affectionate to the sons
      Vatsala — affectionate, from vatsa (calf). The Gauḍīya rasa-name 'bhakta-vatsala' (affectionate to His devotees) draws on the same root. Yaśodā is vatsalā to Kṛṣṇa; Kṛṣṇa is vatsala to all who love Him — the verb is mutual, the love bidirectional.
    Because of being too attached to playing with the other boys, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma did not return upon being called by Rohiṇī. Therefore Rohiṇī sent mother Yaśodā to call Them back, because mother Yaśodā was more affectionate to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
    Purport

    Yaśodāṁ preṣayām āsa. These very words show that since Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma did not care to return in response to the order of Rohiṇī, Rohiṇī thought that if Yaśodā called They would have to return, for Yaśodā was more affectionate to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Because of being too attached to playing with the other boys, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma did not return upon being called by Rohiṇī. Therefore Rohiṇī sent mother Yaśodā to call Them back, because mother Yaśodā was more affectionate to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
    Commentary

    When they did not come, Rohini sent Yasoda because she felt that Yasoda had more affection for the two boys and could therefore attract them.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Rohiṇī called them, and then she sent Yaśodā since Yaśodā was able to attract them quickly because of her greater affection. Why did she call them? She had affection for her son. She also feared accidents on the bank of the river, and wanted to bath and feed the two boys.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma did not come to her because they were attached to playing with their friends, she sent Yaśodā, since with her great affection she was capable of grabbing them by their hands and bringing them back. Why did she to this? She was affectionate to the two boys. She wanted to bathe and feed them.

    Personal Guidance
    When duty's call goes unheeded, the heart that loves most is sent — Kṛṣṇa yields to vātsalya, showing that bhakti through affection draws Him where command cannot.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you respond to love but resist mere authority — and offer that softness back to Kṛṣṇa as the doorway of bhakti.
    • When you must call someone (a child, a junior, a friend) away from their absorption, lead with affection rather than command, modeling Yaśodā's pull over Rohiṇī's order.
    • Refuse the impersonal posture in your sādhana today — speak to Kṛṣṇa as Yaśodā's son who comes when called with love, not as a distant Absolute.
    Analogy

    An officer's whistle is ignored by playing children, but the mother's voice, soft and pitched with milk, brings them running — command is a chain, affection is a thread, and the thread holds Kṛṣṇa where the chain cannot. Rohiṇī sends Yaśodā because she knows that vātsalya-prema travels where authority falls flat.

    Stories
    Yaśodā chosen over Rohiṇī

    The Bhāgavatam's narrator notes precisely that Yaśodā was 'putra-vatsalā' — more affectionate to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma than Rohiṇī was. The text is not making an emotional ranking; it is staging a theological point.

    Gauḍīya commentators: in śāstra, when two devotees stand in the same scene, the one named with the deeper rasa-attribute draws Kṛṣṇa more strongly. Yaśodā's vātsalya-snuta-stana (verse 14) is itself the rope by which He is drawn home — stronger than Rohiṇī's voice, stronger than any command. Love outranks authority in Bhagavān's economy.

    Important Words
    • ajohavīt — called repeatedly
      An intensive (frequentative) verbal form of hū (to call) — 'kept calling, called over and over.' The grammatical doubling captures vātsalya's restless repetition. Gauḍīya commentators love this verb: prema does not call once and quit; it calls again and again, like the gopīs' kīrtana of Kṛṣṇa-nāma.
    • ati - velam — although it was too late
      Ati-velā — past the proper hour. Time-pressure is the practical hinge: even Yaśodā's love operates inside dharma's clock (meals on time, baths before sunset). Bhakti does not abolish proper sequence; it enacts proper sequence with maximum tenderness.
    • saha - agrajam — with His elder brother
      Agraja — first-born, elder. Balarāma is always agraja to Kṛṣṇa in Vraja-līlā. Gauḍīya theology: Balarāma is the original guru-tattva, the first expansion of Kṛṣṇa, and His elder-presence in every scene marks the principle that bhakti always travels with guru.
    • putra - sneha - snuta - stanī — milk flowing from her breast from love for her son
      A compound that compresses three things into one image: putra (son), sneha (affection), snuta (flowing), stanī (with breast). Gauḍīya rasa-śāstra cites this exact phrase as evidence that vātsalya-rasa has its own sāttvika-bhāva — milk-flow — alongside the eight standard ones. The compound is a technical citation.
    Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, being attached to Their play, were playing with the other boys although it was very late. Therefore mother Yaśodā called Them back for lunch. Because of her ecstatic love and affection for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, milk flowed from her breasts.
    Purport

    The word ajohavīt means “calling them again and again.” “Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma,” she called, “please come back. You are late for Your lunch. You have played sufficiently. Come back.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, being attached to Their play, were playing with the other boys although it was very late. Therefore mother Yaśodā called Them back for lunch. Because of her ecstatic love and affection for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, milk flowed from her breasts.
    Commentary

    She began to call repeatedly (ajohavit). She called from far off, because she feared that if she came close they would run away.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She called them repeatedly. She did not come close, fearing they would run away.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Her heart overcome with indescribable affection (sā), she called out many times (ativelam) to Kṛṣṇa who was playing with the boys (bālaiḥ saha). Or she called to Kṛṣṇa, her son and Balarāma, his elder brother, because it was getting late (ativelam). Or seeing him with Balarāma (sāgrajam), she called out.

      His Holiness Romapada Swami· 2020-06-17· English
    Personal Guidance
    Yaśodā's milk-flowing call shows prema in action — Kṛṣṇa is bound by a mother's love, and our devotion ripens when service becomes that personal.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one relationship today where duty has gone cold, and re-enter it with the bodily warmth of vātsalya — call, feed, wait — instead of merely managing it.
    • When you call someone back from their absorption (a child from play, a friend from distraction), do it ajohavīt — again and again, without irritation, as Yaśodā called Kṛṣṇa.
    • Refuse the modern cult of detachment-as-coldness: today, let yourself be visibly moved — in prayer, in service, in love for Kṛṣṇa — without performing composure.
    Analogy

    When a mother calls her child, her voice is not merely sound but body — milk lets down, hands open, breath catches. Yaśodā calls Kṛṣṇa and prema flows from her breasts visibly; love in Vraja is not concept but physiology, and Bhagavān answers what is offered with the body, not just the mind.

    Stories
    Devahūti hearing Kapila

    When Devahūti listened to her son Kapila expound sāṅkhya and bhakti (SB 3.25–33), her body too responded — tears flowing, voice catching, the same vātsalya-prema overflowing as physiology, not merely thought. The Bhāgavatam consistently treats bodily response as evidence of rasa's reality.

    Gauḍīya tradition codifies this in the eight sāttvika-bhāvas (stambha, sveda, romāñca, svara-bheda, vepathu, vaivarṇya, aśru, pralaya). Yaśodā's flowing milk in this verse is read as the vātsalya-sister of those eight: prema made visible in the body. The 'modern cult of detachment-as-coldness' the personal-guidance file flags is exactly what Gauḍīya tradition opposes.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa aravinda - akṣa — O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O lotus-eyed one
      The doubled vocative + epithet. Gauḍīya nāma-tattva: even Yaśodā's domestic call is nāma-kīrtana. To name Him 'aravindākṣa' (lotus-eyed) is to attribute to Him the very imagery used in Bhagavān-meditation. The household call and the sādhaka's meditation use the same words.
    • tāta — O darling
      Tāta — a term used both for father and for beloved child, depending on direction. In Yaśodā's mouth, addressing Kṛṣṇa, it is the down-direction (beloved son). Gauḍīya commentators note the rasa-poetry: the same word that would call a father here calls the Father of all as a son.
    • stanam — the milk of my breast
      Stana — breast. The Gauḍīya rasa-śāstra holds that Yaśodā's breast-milk has an exceptional status: it has nourished svayaṁ-bhagavān, and through that contact has become an object of vātsalya-rasa-meditation in itself. Sevā at the bodily level is not lower than at the mental level — it is its own register.
    • krīḍā - śrāntaḥ — fatigued from playing
      Śrānta — wearied. Bhagavān 'tires' — naravat-līlā again. Gauḍīya commentators: His apparent fatigue is the doorway through which Yaśodā can serve. Without this concession, vātsalya-sevā would have no foothold.
    Mother Yaśodā said: My dear son Kṛṣṇa, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, come here and drink the milk of my breast. My dear darling, You must be very tired because of hunger and the fatigue of playing so long. There is no need to play any more.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Mother Yaśodā said: My dear son Kṛṣṇa, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, come here and drink the milk of my breast. My dear darling, You must be very tired because of hunger and the fatigue of playing so long. There is no need to play any more.
    Commentary

    She repeated several times his name from far off, so that he would hear.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She repeatedly called him so he could hear from far away and also to reveal her obstinacy. She called with affection “O lotus eyed boy!” to make him come quickly. Though she was actually afraid for their safety she said they must be tired and hungry since she was worried about telling anything inauspicious to them (like danger from demons). She thought that Balarāma would bring him by force since he followed her orders. Thus she called Balarāma.

    Personal Guidance
    Mother Yaśodā's call reveals Kṛṣṇa's sweetness as bhakta-vatsala — the Supreme accepts intimate sevā from one bound to Him by pure love.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today the moments when someone offers you food, rest, or care, and receive it as Kṛṣṇa receives Yaśodā's milk — without ego, with sweetness.
    • Render one act of bodily sevā (cooking, feeding, tending) to a devotee or family member, offering it inwardly to Kṛṣṇa as Yaśodā would.
    • Refuse the impersonalist habit of treating Kṛṣṇa as abstract; speak to Him today by name as Yaśodā did — 'kṛṣṇa, kṛṣṇa, aravindākṣa' — in plain, personal address.
    Analogy

    A queen, robed and crowned, kneels by her hungry child and offers her own breast — the throne is unmoved, the dynasty unaltered, but for this hour the empire shrinks to a milk-cup. Yaśodā calls Kṛṣṇa lotus-eyed, weary from play, and offers her body's milk to Bhagavān; vātsalya scales the cosmos down to a mother's lap.

    Stories
    Putanā and the antidote

    Pūtanā gave Kṛṣṇa a breast smeared with poison and was liberated because the act was outwardly mother-like (SB 10.6). Yaśodā gives Kṛṣṇa a breast filled with prema-laden milk, and the scene is the very paradigm of Vraja-vātsalya.

    Gauḍīya commentators (Rūpa Gosvāmī in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu) treat the two scenes as deliberately paired: Pūtanā's act receives Kṛṣṇa's mercy because of its outward form; Yaśodā's act is the rasa that Pūtanā only counterfeited. Recognizing the distinction is part of training in mādhurya- and vātsalya-rasa.

    Important Words
    • he rāma — O Balarāma
      Vocative with the particle 'he' — formal address. Yaśodā calls Balarāma first and formally before calling Kṛṣṇa. Gauḍīya teaching: even in Vraja's most intimate love, the senior is addressed first. This is the seed of the sampradāya principle of approaching Kṛṣṇa through Balarāma (the original guru-tattva).
    • āśu — immediately
      Āśu — quickly, without delay. The same word the Gītā uses for swift action (BG 4.39: śraddhāvāl labhate jñānaṁ … āśu). Yaśodā's call invokes the same urgency: when love calls, delay is the only impropriety.
    • kula - nandana — delight of the family
      Kula-nandana — He who gives delight (nanda) to the kula (family line). Balarāma is so addressed because His mere presence sustains the family's spiritual atmosphere. Gauḍīya tradition: every family that hopes to hold bhakti needs a Balarāma-figure — a senior who anchors and delights.
    • kṛta - āhāraḥ — having eaten
      A compound — 'one for whom eating has been done.' The grammatical passive matters: in Vraja, Kṛṣṇa's eating is Yaśodā's act as much as His. The doer is the offerer; the recipient is the Lord; bhakti dissolves the line between.
    My dear Baladeva, best of our family, please come immediately with Your younger brother, Kṛṣṇa. You both ate in the morning, and now You ought to eat something more.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear Baladeva, best of our family, please come immediately with Your younger brother, Kṛṣṇa. You both ate in the morning, and now You ought to eat something more.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She addressed Balarāma as the son of the dynasty, so that Kṛṣṇa would come quickly out of envy. It can also be an address to him. Another version has krīḍā-śrānto si putraka: O son! You are tired from playing. Putraka (little son) indicates a show of mercy out of affection.

    Personal Guidance
    Yaśodā's call to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa to come eat reveals that the Supreme accepts the seva of those who love Him in vātsalya — pure parental affection.
    Practical Applications
    • Offer your next meal to Kṛṣṇa with the affection of one feeding a beloved child, not the formality of a ritual checklist.
    • Notice when you serve others (family, juniors, dependents) with calculation, and replace it today with the unconditional care Yaśodā shows here.
    • Refuse the impersonalist habit of treating Kṛṣṇa as an abstraction — speak to Him directly, by name, the way mother Yaśodā calls 'tāta, āśu, āgaccha.'
    Analogy

    A grandmother calls both grandchildren in from the field — the older one first, by his honorific, because addressing the senior with respect is itself how you reach the junior who walks at his side. Yaśodā summons Rāma as kula-nandana, knowing Kṛṣṇa walks beside Him, and bhakti always honors the elder to reach the beloved.

    Stories
    Balarāma honored first

    Throughout the Tenth Canto, Yaśodā addresses Balarāma with formal honorifics — kula-nandana, dāśārha, Rāma — even as she calls Kṛṣṇa with intimate diminutives (tāta, putraka, aravindākṣa). The grammatical asymmetry is doctrinal.

    Gauḍīya theology: Balarāma is Kṛṣṇa's original ādi-guru and elder; even in the most intimate vātsalya-rasa, He is approached through the register of respect, while Kṛṣṇa is approached through the register of love. Devotees who skip over Balarāma — and gurus generally — to reach Kṛṣṇa miss the structure that Yaśodā herself observes.

    Important Words
    • pratīkṣate — is waiting
      Prati-īkṣ — to look toward, await. Nanda is actively looking-out-for, not merely delayed. The Gauḍīya reading: Bhagavān is also pratīkṣamāṇa — He waits for His devotees too. Nanda's waiting is the human face of Kṛṣṇa's own.
    • dāśārha — O Balarāma (descendant of Daśārha)
      Dāśārha — of the Daśārha line (Yadu dynasty). The honorific names Balarāma's noble lineage, dignifying the call. Gauḍīya commentators: even in the simplest household summons, lineage is preserved — bhakti does not abolish vaṁśa but completes it.
    • vraja - adhipaḥ — the King of Vraja
      Adhipa — overlord, king. Nanda is Vraja's king and also Kṛṣṇa's father. The Gauḍīya theology: in Vraja, kingship and fatherhood collapse into one role because the king's child is the Supreme. Adhipatya is service when the throne serves Kṛṣṇa.
    • sva - gṛhān — to their own homes
      Sva-gṛha — one's own home. The verse closes with Yaśodā ensuring the other boys go home — care for them is not optional politeness but part of her vātsalya. Gauḍīya teaching: real love does not absorb the beloved away from his other duties; it sends everyone home cared-for.
    Nanda Mahārāja, the King of Vraja, is now waiting to eat. O my dear son Balarāma, he is waiting for You. Therefore, come back to please us. All the boys playing with You and Kṛṣṇa should now go to their homes.
    Purport

    It appears that Nanda Mahārāja regularly took his food with his two sons, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Yaśodā told the other boys, “Now you should go to your homes.” Father and son generally sit together, so mother Yaśodā requested Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to return, and she advised the other boys to go home so that their parents would not have to wait for them.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Nanda Mahārāja, the King of Vraja, is now waiting to eat. O my dear son Balarāma, he is waiting for You. Therefore, come back to please us. All the boys playing with You and Kṛṣṇa should now go to their homes.
    Commentary

    "Your father is sitting but without you he cannot eat (bhoksyaman.) Why are you giving your father hunger pangs? All you boys should go to your houses. Your parents are also in difficulty like us. Please make them happy." She said all this to stop them from playing.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O descendent of Dāśārha! Nanda, thinking highly of you as the son of his friend, will not eat without you. Make Rohiṇī and myself happy, or make Nanda and myself happy. Seeing Balarāma absorbed in playing out of prema for Kṛṣṇa, who was attached to playing, she ordered the other boys to go home. She did not mention the individual homes of the other boys (sva-sva-gṛheṣu) because she spoke quickly. Seeing the other boys did not go home because of their affection for Kṛṣṇa, she falsely called him for a special reason.

    Personal Guidance
    Even Kṛṣṇa returns home when called to the family meal — honor the small daily duties that hold household life together.
    Practical Applications
    • Show up for one shared family meal today without phone, work, or distraction — simply eat together as Kṛṣṇa did with Nanda Mahārāja.
    • Notice when you keep parents or housemates waiting on small things, and refuse the self-importance that says your task matters more than their peace of mind.
    • Before leaving any gathering today, send the others home gently and on time, the way Yaśodā did — care for them includes not letting their people worry.
    Analogy

    Even the universe's host pauses to be present at His own father's plate — the king of the entire dynasty waits for his sons to come home to eat, and the proper order of the household holds even Kṛṣṇa within it. Nanda's pratīkṣā (waiting) is itself a form of seva that the Lord honors by coming.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa eating with Nanda in Vraja

    Throughout Vraja-līlā, Kṛṣṇa shares meals with Nanda Mahārāja in a way He does not later share with anyone in Mathurā or Dvārakā. The Gauḍīya saints (especially Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmī in Vraja-vilāsa-stava) meditate on these meals as among the most poignant rasa-tableaux of all līlā.

    The verse's small instruction — Nanda is waiting; come — is the household scaffolding inside which the highest rasa is staged. Gauḍīya tradition: the seemingly mundane discipline (eating at the right time, with the right elder) is the trellis on which prema climbs. Without trellis, the vine falls.

    Important Words
    • majjanam āvaha — now take Your bath
      Majjana — immersion, bath. The same root as majj (to plunge). Gauḍīya commentators see this as the daily seed of dīkṣā: regular bodily śuddhi prepares the consciousness for the inner śuddhi of mantra-japa. Bhakti honors the body's role; it does not skip it.
    • janma - ṛkṣam — the auspicious star of Your birth
      Janma-ṛkṣa — the nakṣatra under which one is born. In Vedic culture, the recurrence of one's birth-star each month is an auspicious day for dāna and observance. Gauḍīya tradition: time itself has structure, and bhakti operates through that structure rather than against it.
    • viprebhyaḥ — unto the brāhmaṇas
      Vipra — the learned brāhmaṇa, specifically. Gauḍīya theology elevates the Vaiṣṇava above the merely-born vipra (na śūdrā bhagavad-bhaktās…), but in this verse the principle is preserved: dāna flows toward those preserving Veda and Kṛṣṇa-jñāna. Today's vipra is the devotee preserving Kṛṣṇa-kathā.
    • dehi — give in charity
      Dehi — imperative of dā (to give). The Gītā's threefold tapaḥ-yajña-dāna (BG 17.20–22) is condensed here in the single act Yaśodā prescribes. The proper sāttvika-dāna is to the deserving, at the proper time, without expectation of return — exactly the structure of this verse.
    • gāḥ — cows
      Go — the cow, central to Vraja's economy and Kṛṣṇa's identity (Govinda, Gopāla). To give cows is to give what Kṛṣṇa Himself protects. Gauḍīya teaching: dāna of cows is dāna into Kṛṣṇa's own household and therefore has special potency on His janma-ṛkṣa.
    • śuciḥ — being purified
      Śuci — pure, bright. Etymologically related to fire (śoc, to shine). Gauḍīya commentators: external śaucha (bath, clean cloth) and internal śaucha (mind fixed on Hari) are not alternatives — the first prepares for the second. The verse asks for both.
    Mother Yaśodā further told Kṛṣṇa: My dear son, because of playing all day, Your body has become covered with dust and sand. Therefore, come back, take Your bath and cleanse Yourself. Today the moon is conjoined with the auspicious star of Your birth. Therefore, be pure and give cows in charity to the brāhmaṇas.
    Purport

    It is a custom of Vedic culture that whenever there is any auspicious ceremony, one should give valuable cows in charity to the brāhmaṇas. Therefore mother Yaśodā requested Kṛṣṇa, “Instead of being enthusiastic in playing, now please come and be enthusiastic in charity.” Yajña-dāna-tapaḥ-karma na tyājyaṁ kāryam eva tat. As advised in Bhagavad-gītā (18.5) , sacrifice, charity and austerity should never be given up. Yajño dānaṁ tapaś caiva pāvanāni manīṣiṇām: even if one is very much advanced in spiritual life, one should not give up these three duties. To observe one’s birthday ceremony, one should do something in terms of one of these three items ( yajña, dāna or tapaḥ ), or all of them together.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Mother Yaśodā further told Kṛṣṇa: My dear son, because of playing all day, Your body has become covered with dust and sand. Therefore, come back, take Your bath and cleanse Yourself. Today the moon is conjoined with the auspicious star of Your birth. Therefore, be pure and give cows in charity to the brāhmaṇas.
    Commentary

    He still did not come. In order to make him give up his enthusiasm for playing she tried to kindle his enthusiasm in giving charity.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Take your bath according to the rules. She made him excited since he was enthusiastic to give gifts. Clean yourself since the moon is in your birth constellation. Instead of bhavati, sometimes bhavataḥ (your) is seen. You are constantly growing. When he still did not come, she showed that the other boys had now gone home, to make him envious.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing that the other boys could give up playing because of affection for Kṛṣṇa, she explained a special purpose in going home. You have to bathe completely (majjanam āvaha). This should be done with water purified by mantras chanted by brāhmaṇas, because today the moon is in Rohiṇī constellation. Instead of bhavati, sometimes bhavataḥ (your) is seen. You are constantly growing. The goal is explained. You have to be pure by bathing in order to give gifts to the brāhmaṇas.

    Personal Guidance
    On auspicious days, pause play and turn to śaucha and dāna — bathe, purify, and give to brāhmaṇas, marking time with yajña, dāna, tapaḥ.
    Practical Applications
    • On your next birthday or auspicious tithi, give something of real value (cows are rare; offer to a brāhmaṇa, temple, or devotee who is preserving Kṛṣṇa-kathā) rather than treating the day as personal celebration.
    • Before sitting for sādhana today, bathe and put on clean cloth — refuse the modern habit of approaching Kṛṣṇa dust-covered from the day's play.
    • Pick one of yajña, dāna, or tapaḥ and perform it deliberately today, so the day is marked by Kṛṣṇa-conscious action and not merely consumed.
    Analogy

    A jeweler does not adorn his greatest gem on an ordinary day; he reserves the polish, the cloth, the offering for a marked star. Yaśodā waits for Kṛṣṇa's birth-star and turns the day into a small yajña — bath, cleansing, brāhmaṇa-dāna, cows. Auspicious time becomes a vessel into which bhakti is poured.

    Stories
    Birthday observances in śāstra

    Throughout the Bhāgavatam, devotees mark birth-stars (janma-nakṣatra) with specific observances: Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira gave cows, gold, and land to brāhmaṇas; Vidura performed tīrtha-yātrā; even Ambarīṣa structured his Ekādaśīs around such observances. The śāstric pattern of dāna on auspicious tithis is not Vedic ritualism — it is bhakti's calendar.

    Gauḍīya tradition continues this through Janmāṣṭamī, Nityānanda Trayodaśī, Gaura Pūrṇimā, and the appearance days of the Six Gosvāmīs. The discipline Yaśodā teaches Kṛṣṇa here — make the marked day a day of dāna and śuddhi — is the same discipline by which the sampradāya marks its sacred calendar.

    Important Words
    • paśya paśya — just see, just see
      Doubled imperative of dṛś (to see). Gauḍīya commentators note the vātsalya-doubling — love repeats itself. The same syntactic pattern appears in Yaśodā's calling 'kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa' (verse 15) and 'sādhu sādhu' (verse 30). Repetition is the grammar of affection.
    • vayasyān — boys of Your age
      Vayasya — age-mates, peers. In Gauḍīya rasa-theology, Kṛṣṇa's vayasyas in Vraja (especially Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Śrīdāmā) are sakhya-rasa eternal associates. The verse's mention of vayasyas thus carries doctrinal weight beyond the immediate scene.
    • mātṛ - mṛṣṭān — cleansed by their mothers
      Mṛṣṭa — wiped clean, polished. The compound emphasizes that the work is done by the mothers, not the boys themselves. Gauḍīya teaching: even bodily care, when done by a devotee's hand, is seva — and the receiver of seva is, ultimately, Kṛṣṇa in the form of the cared-for child.
    • su - alaṅkṛtān — well decorated
      Su-alaṅkṛta — beautifully ornamented. Alaṅkāra is one of the elements of Kṛṣṇa's worship in Vraja: the Deity is dressed and decorated daily. Even the children's dressing is a domestic echo of arcana — the household running on Vraja's rhythms of bath, dress, feed.
    Just see how all Your playmates of Your own age have been cleansed and decorated with beautiful ornaments by their mothers. You should come here, and after You have taken Your bath, eaten Your lunch and been decorated with ornaments, You may play with Your friends again.
    Purport

    Generally young boys are competitive. If one friend has done something, another friend also wants to do something. Therefore mother Yaśodā pointed out how Kṛṣṇa’s playmates were decorated, so that Kṛṣṇa might be induced to decorate Himself like them.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya

    Just see how all Your playmates of Your own age have been cleansed and decorated with beautiful ornaments by their mothers. You should come here, and after You have taken Your bath, eaten Your lunch and been decorated with ornaments, You may play with Your friends again.
    Commentary

    When he still did not come, she tried to generate envy in him by showing the example of the other boys.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She repeats the word paśya as an expression of scolding, anger or lamentation arising from prema. See your friends who have been cleansed by their mothers by bathing etc. and then nicely ornamented.

    Personal Guidance
    Mother Yaśodā uses a child's natural competitiveness to draw Kṛṣṇa toward bath, food, and ornament — affection knows how to make sādhana attractive.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one healthy peer-comparison today and let it pull you toward sādhana — earlier rising, cleaner chanting — rather than toward viṣaya.
    • Before sitting for japa or study, take a proper bath and eat a sāttvika meal, treating bodily care as Yaśodā's loving prelude to service, not a distraction from it.
    • Speak to a younger person in your life the way mother Yaśodā speaks to Kṛṣṇa — coaxing, specific, affectionate — instead of issuing abstract moral commands.
    Analogy

    A mother does not lecture her playing child on cleanliness in the abstract; she points to the bright neighbor-boy and says, 'See how they are dressed.' Healthy comparison is bait, not poison — Yaśodā uses Kṛṣṇa's natural delight in being seen and praised to draw Him toward bath, food, and ornament. Sādhana is more often coaxed than commanded.

    Stories
    Caitanya's coaxing of the renunciants

    Caitanya Mahāprabhu, gathering the Six Gosvāmīs in Vṛndāvana, did not command their renunciation; He coaxed each of them — Rūpa and Sanātana through dialogue at Rāmakeli, Raghunātha dāsa through years of waiting, Gopāla Bhaṭṭa through a vision — using the natural affinities of each soul as the bait toward sādhana.

    Gauḍīya tradition: the higher the bhakti, the more skillfully it appeals to what each person already loves. Yaśodā's pointing at the well-dressed playmates is the household-scale of the same principle that the ācāryas use to draw souls to Kṛṣṇa: meet the child where he is, then walk him home.

    Important Words
    • tam aśeṣa - śekharam — Him, the crown of all
      Aśeṣa-śekhara — crest of all that is. The verse insists on Kṛṣṇa's supreme position precisely in the moment of His being bathed and dressed by His mother. Gauḍīya theology demands this co-presence: were He less than aśeṣa-śekhara, the rasa would collapse into mere sentiment.
    • matvā — considering
      Past active participle of man (to think) — 'having considered.' Yaśodā 'considers' Kṛṣṇa her son. The Gauḍīya gloss: this consideration is not a cognitive error; it is yoga-māyā-supported truth at the rasa-level. He genuinely is her son in Vraja, while remaining svayaṁ-bhagavān at the tattva-level.
    • sneha - nibaddha - dhīḥ — with intelligence bound by affection
      A precise rasa-compound: dhī (intelligence) ni-baddha (bound) by sneha (affection). The Gauḍīya teaching: prema does not bypass the intellect — it binds it, redirects it. Yaśodā's intellect, fully functional, is in service of her sneha rather than against it. This is the integration prema produces.
    • acyutam — Kṛṣṇa, the infallible
      Acyuta — never-falling. The verse twice marks His Godhood (aśeṣa-śekharam, acyutam) inside the act of being led home by the hand. The grammatical insistence is the doctrinal point: He is led, He is bathed, He is fed — and He remains acyuta throughout.
    • kṛtavatī — performed
      Past active participle, feminine — 'she having performed.' The active voice is hers; she is the doer of His bath, dress, feeding. Gauḍīya theology: Yaśodā's kartṛtva (doership) here is real seva, not a stage-show. The Lord receives doership from His devotees by allowing them this role.
    My dear Mahārāja Parīkṣit, because of intense love and affection, mother Yaśodā, Kṛṣṇa’s mother, considered Kṛṣṇa, who was at the peak of all opulences, to be her own son. Thus she took Kṛṣṇa by the hand, along with Balarāma, and brought Them home, where she performed her duties by fully bathing Them, dressing Them and feeding Them.
    Purport

    Kṛṣṇa is always neat, clean and opulent and does not need to be washed, bathed or dressed, yet mother Yaśodā, because of affection, considered Him her ordinary child and did her duties to keep her son brilliant.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear Mahārāja Parīkṣit, because of intense love and affection, mother Yaśodā, Kṛṣṇa's mother, considered Kṛṣṇa, who was at the peak of all opulences, to be her own son. Thus she took Kṛṣṇa by the hand, along with Balarāma, and brought Them home, where she performed her duties by fully bathing Them, dressing Them and feeding Them.
    Commentary

    She thought of the crest jewel of Ananta, the source of all avataras (asesa sekharam), as her son. Another meaning is: she considered him not as bhagavan (a- sesasekharam). Actually he was both. Another meaning could be: she thought of her son as the crest jewel of the entirety (asesa) of their family. Taking him to his house (sva batam) she made him bathe, eat and then decorated him (udayan).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse summarizes her actions. Approaching slowly while uttering affectionate words, thinking of him as her son though he was to the head ornament of unlimited avatāras, her intelligence controlled intensely by affection, she took him by the hand though he was playing. She brought him back to her house (svabāṭam) in a way that he could not escape (acyutam) and performed auspicious acts (udayam) such as bathing, feeding and ornamenting him. Or she performed the festive rites suitable to his birth star, for which he was eager, as she had mentioned previously. She did this immediately (atha) or completely. Śukadeva addresses Parīkṣit with “O King!” Nrpa means the protector of the people. He addresses Parīkṣit with affection, on seeing Parīkṣit’s manifestation of affection for Kṛṣṇa. śrī-śuka uvāca gopa-vṛddhā mahotpātān anubhūya bṛhadvane nandādayaḥ samāgamya vraja-kāryam amantrayan śrī-śukaḥ uvāca—Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said; gopa-vṛddhāḥ—the elderly persons among the cowherd men; mahā-utpātān—very great disturbances; anubhūya—after experiencing; bṛhadvane—in the place known as Bṛhadvana; nanda-ādayaḥ—the cowherd men, headed by Nanda Mahārāja; samāgamya—assembled, came together; vraja-kāryam—the business of Vrajabhūmi; amantrayan—deliberated on how to stop the continuous disturbances in Mahāvana.

    Personal Guidance
    Even Kṛṣṇa, the peak of all opulences, accepts a devotee's loving sevā as her son — He is conquered by vātsalya-bhakti, not by power.
    Practical Applications
    • Choose one small act of sevā today (cooking, cleaning, dressing the Deity or serving a guest as Kṛṣṇa) and perform it with the conviction that He personally accepts it.
    • Refuse the modern cynicism that sevā is merely 'symbolic' — bathe, dress, and feed Kṛṣṇa (or those entrusted to your care) as Yaśodā did, with shaucha and tenderness, not as a chore.
    • Notice when you withhold affection because someone 'doesn't need it' — give it anyway, the way Yaśodā bathed the already-pure Lord, and let love, not utility, govern your duty.
    Analogy

    An empress washing the feet of her own son — even though those feet are worshipped by all the gods — would not feel her affection diminished by His glory; if anything it would deepen, because she alone holds Him by the right of love. Yaśodā considers aśeṣa-śekhara (the crown of everything) her own son, and serves Him at full domestic detail: hand-led home, bathed, dressed, fed.

    Stories
    Yaśodā binding Kṛṣṇa (Dāmodara)

    The most famous icon of this verse's principle is the Dāmodara-līlā: Yaśodā tries to tie the toddler Kṛṣṇa to the mortar, and the rope keeps falling exactly two fingers short — until her love exhausts her and Kṛṣṇa allows the binding. Sanātana Gosvāmī's Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta and the Caitanya-caritāmṛta both treat this scene as the highest aiśvarya of Bhagavān: that He, who is uncontainable, makes Himself containable by a devotee's prema.

    The present verse's 'aśeṣa-śekharam … sneha-nibaddha-dhīḥ' is the same revelation in domestic form: He is the crown of all opulence; her dhī (intellect) is bound by sneha; she serves Him as her son. Both halves are simultaneously true — acintya-bhedābheda in its rasa-form.

    Important Words
    • gopa - vṛddhāḥ — the elderly cowherd men
      Vṛddha — grown, mature, elder. Not merely 'old' but 'matured by experience.' Gauḍīya teaching: vṛddhatva is not chronological age but ripeness in dharma and bhakti. The Bhāgavatam consistently directs decisions to the vṛddhas because the elder has the long view.
    • mahā - utpātān — the great disturbances
      Mahā-utpāta — great portents, alarming omens. The same word used by the gopas earlier for Kṛṣṇa's līlā (verse 3). Gauḍīya teaching: utpātas are real and require response, but the response is consultation, not panic.
    • bṛhadvane — in Bṛhadvana (Mahāvana)
      Bṛhadvana — 'the great forest,' the original Gokula. The locative case fixes the scene. Gauḍīya geography: each named site of Vraja carries its own rasa, and the migration from Bṛhadvana to Vṛndāvana (forthcoming in verse 28) is a passage from one rasa-stratum to another.
    • samāgamya — having assembled
      Sam-ā-gam — to come together. The verb of saṅga itself. Even before the deliberation begins, the act of coming-together is the first sādhana. Gauḍīya theology: sat-saṅga precedes correct discernment; the right counsel emerges from the right assembly.
    • vraja - kāryam — the business of Vraja
      Kārya — that which is to be done, a duty. The duty here is rakṣā of the bhakti-community. Gauḍīya teaching: every saṅga has its kārya — the practical sva-dharma of preserving and extending Kṛṣṇa-consciousness — and elders meet specifically to discern that kārya.
    Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Then one time, having seen the great disturbances in Bṛhadvana, all the elderly persons among the cowherd men, headed by Nanda Mahārāja, assembled and began to consider what to do to stop the continuous disturbing situations in Vraja.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Then one time, having seen the great disturbances in Bṛhadvana, all the elderly persons among the cowherd men, headed by Nanda Mahārāja, assembled and began to consider what to do to stop the continuous disturbing situations in Vraja.
    Commentary

    After playing in Mahavana, when Krsna desired to play in Vrndavana, Upananda suggested that they all move to Vrndavana.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    svābhāvikena tat premnā gopa-puṅgavāḥ hary-eka-maṅgalāhāryam vrajakāryam amantrayan The men of Vraja, inspired by their natural prema, the best of the cowherds consulted about moving Vraja for Kṛṣṇa’s welfare. They met together in an assembly after the breaking of the arjuna trees and a sacrifice to Indra and discussed what should be done for the welfare of Kṛṣṇa, the life of Vraja (vajra-kāryam).

    Personal Guidance
    When disturbances mount in your sphere of care, gather the wise elders and deliberate — protection of Kṛṣṇa's devotees is a collective sva-dharma.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one recurring 'disturbance' in your household or community today, and instead of reacting alone, convene the elders or seniors who hold responsibility with you.
    • Refuse the modern instinct to act as a lone solver — bring at least one trusted senior into a decision you would normally make in isolation.
    • Speak to an elder in your family or saṅga today and ask their counsel on a protective duty (rakṣā) you have been carrying silently.
    Analogy

    When a storm threatens the herd, the chief cowherd does not run out alone with a stick — he calls the elders to the fire and consults. Care for Kṛṣṇa and the community is collective work: Nanda gathers the gopa-vṛddhas because rakṣaṇa (protection) is a sva-dharma to be discharged by counsel, not by lone heroism.

    Stories
    Yudhiṣṭhira's councils

    Throughout the Mahābhārata, before any major decision — Rajasūya-yajña, the war, the Aśvamedha — Yudhiṣṭhira convenes the elders: Bhīṣma, Vidura, Kṛṣṇa, Vyāsa, the Kumāras when present. He never moves alone. The śāstric pattern: when responsibility is large, council is dharma.

    Gauḍīya tradition extends this to the saṅga itself. Caitanya Mahāprabhu commissioned the Six Gosvāmīs as a body — not one master — to recover and systematize Vraja. Nanda's gathering the gopa-vṛddhas in this verse is the household-scale of the same principle: serious protection of bhakti's environment is a collective work, not a private one.

    Important Words
    • upananda - nāmā — by the name Upananda
      Upananda — 'near Nanda,' Nanda's elder brother. In Vraja-vaṁśa, Upananda is the eldest brother of the five Nanda-brothers and a recognized authority on Vraja's affairs. The Gauḍīya commentators identify him as the natural sabhā-leader — older even than Nanda himself.
    • jñāna - vayaḥ - adhikaḥ — senior in knowledge and age
      A double qualification: jñāna (knowledge) and vayas (age), with adhika (greater) marking superiority in both. Gauḍīya teaching: vayas alone is not authority; jñāna alone is not authority; both together produce the elder whose counsel śāstra honors.
    • deśa - kāla - artha - tattva - jñaḥ — knower of place, time, situation, and reality
      A four-fold compound. Deśa (place), kāla (time), artha (circumstance or purpose), tattva (the underlying truth). Gauḍīya teaching: practical bhakti requires discernment in all four dimensions. Yukta-vairāgya (Rūpa Gosvāmī) is exactly this — fitting the practice to place, time, situation, and the soul's actual condition.
    • priya - kṛt — doer of what is dear
      Priya-kṛt — one who does what is beloved (to Rāma-Kṛṣṇa, the protected pair). Gauḍīya theology: the highest motivation in any decision is what is priya to Bhagavān. Upananda's authority comes from being oriented to Kṛṣṇa's pleasure, not to his own faction.
    At this meeting of all the inhabitants of Gokula, a cowherd man named Upananda, who was the most mature in age and knowledge and was very experienced according to time, circumstances and country, made this suggestion for the benefit of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    At this meeting of all the inhabitants of Gokula, a cowherd man named Upananda, who was the most mature in age and knowledge and was very experienced according to time, circumstances and country, made this suggestion for the benefit of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    Upananda was Nanda’s elder minister. From the description it is understood that he was wise.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Among them (tatra) Upananda had knowledge of purpose (artha), place and time, taking them individually and all together and had special knowledge of what was best, average and inferior. He was called most knowledgeable (jṣānādhikaḥ). Because he was older and acted according to his name (upa-nanda—subordinate to Nanda) he was Nanda’s advisor and elder brother. This means he was qualified to speak. By his natural prema, he did what was beneficial for Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa (priya-kṛt). He feared for the safety of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, as mentioned in the previous verse (mahotpātān anubhūya). Though actually the name Upananda should be given to the younger brother, their father had named them in the opposite way at his discretion. His father named him Upananda because he gave joy to those close by. Later he named the younger child Nanda as part of the pair. By chance those names happened to describe their position in relation to each other. (Nanda was the main brother, and Upananda was his assistant.) Since Nanda was endowed with all characteristics, Upananda, the elder, most wise brother, voluntarily gave Nanda leadership of Gokula.

    Personal Guidance
    Real leadership in a crisis comes from the elder who is grounded in deśa-kāla-pātra and acts for Kṛṣṇa's protection, not for his own voice.
    Practical Applications
    • When a hard decision sits before your family or sangha today, defer first to the eldest who has shown deśa-kāla-artha-tattva-jña — knowledge of time, place, and circumstance — before offering your own view.
    • Before speaking in any group conflict, ask yourself: 'Is this priya-kṛt for Kṛṣṇa and His devotees?' — and stay silent if it is not.
    • Notice one elder in your life whose maturity you have been quietly dismissing, and seek their counsel on a real decision before the day ends.
    Analogy

    When the council convenes, the right voice is not the loudest but the eldest who has watched the weather of every season — Upananda speaks because he knows time, place, and circumstance, and his counsel is priya-kṛt for the protected children. Real leadership in a crisis is grounded in deśa-kāla-pātra-jñāna, not in personal forcefulness.

    Stories
    Vidura's counsel

    Throughout the Mahābhārata's Udyoga-parva, Vidura — older, wiser, and aligned with dharma — is the one whose counsel Dhṛtarāṣṭra most needed and most ignored. His position parallels Upananda's exactly: a senior with deśa-kāla-artha-tattva-jñāna, speaking for the benefit of the protected innocents (Pāṇḍavas / Rāma-Kṛṣṇa).

    Gauḍīya tradition prizes such elders. Rūpa Gosvāmī, in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu, lists the qualities of a guru in language remarkably close to Upananda's description: knowledgeable, mature, well-disposed toward devotees, capable of discerning what is priya-kṛt for them. The verse's epithet is a quiet portrait of guru-tattva.

    Important Words
    • utthātavyam — this place should be left
      Verbal adjective of ut-sthā (to rise up, depart) — 'is to be risen-from.' The word carries the connotation of leaving behind, not running from. Gauḍīya teaching: relocation for bhakti is an ut-sthāna (rising), not a palāyana (flight).
    • hita - eṣibhiḥ — by those who desire the good
      Hita-eṣin — seeker of welfare. The instrumental plural marks the agents: those who genuinely want Gokula's welfare are precisely the ones who must leave it. Gauḍīya paradox: real love for a place sometimes requires departing from it, when the place has become unsafe for what matters.
    • mahā - utpātāḥ — great disturbances
      The same word from verses 3 and 21. The repetition is structural: the utpātas the gopas first mistook for portents have, by the council's discernment, been re-read as deliberate assault. Gauḍīya teaching: the same external events reveal different meanings as one's discernment matures.
    • bālānām — for the boys
      Genitive plural — 'of the boys.' Specifically Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the protected. Gauḍīya theology: even when Kṛṣṇa is svayaṁ-bhagavān, His Vraja-līlā permits Him to be 'protected' by His devotees. This is bhakta-vaśya's most touching aspect — He accepts being kept safe by those who love Him.
    • nāśa - hetavaḥ — having destruction as their cause
      Nāśa — destruction; hetu — cause, motive. The utpātas are not accidents; they have a hetu, an intentional source. Gauḍīya commentators: this is the bridge to Upananda's reasoning. Disturbances with intent require strategic response (relocation), not merely better defense in place.
    He said: My dear friends the cowherd men, in order to do good to this place, Gokula, we should leave it, because so many disturbances are always occurring here, just for the purpose of killing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    He said: My dear friends the cowherd men, in order to do good to this place, Gokula, we should leave it, because so many disturbances are always occurring here, just for the purpose of killing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    "Thinking of the welfare of all the inhabitants of Vraja (gokulasya hitaisibhih), we should move."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    We should go elsewhere. Why? We think of the benefit of all the people of Gokula. Great disturbances which may cause the destruction of the young boys take place. He mentions boys in general rather than Kṛṣṇa so that Nanda would not feel Kṛṣṇa alone was the cause of moving. Another version has prajānām (all the people). Another version has vrajānām (people of Vraja). In reality by looking after the welfare of Kṛṣṇa all others’ welfare would prosper. While describing the pain of the disturbances to all the people, he showed affection for Kṛṣṇa, who had come there out of curiosity, by putting him on his lap, and spoke of the past incidents concerning Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    We should go elsewhere. Why? We think of the benefit of all the people of Gokula. By giving benefit to Kṛṣṇa everyone benefited. Though the real goal was Kṛṣṇa, as explained later, Upananda mentioned danger to all the boys since they would go quickly if all the cowherds became frightened. Or if Kṛṣṇa was in danger, it followed that all the boys were in danger. Another version has prajānām instead of bālānām. The meaning is the same. Another version has vrajānām. If there was danger to Kṛṣṇa, the life of all beings in Vraja, everyone in Vraja would be destroyed.

    Personal Guidance
    When a place becomes hostile to Kṛṣṇa-conscious life, true daya for the community is to relocate — protect the shelter of the devotees, not the comfort of the spot.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one environment in your life that keeps producing disturbances to your sādhana, and decide today what concrete step Nanda-like resolve would take.
    • Speak to your family or close devotee circle about a 'Gokula-shift' you have been postponing — a move, a job change, a cut friendship — for the sake of Kṛṣṇa's shelter.
    • Refuse the sentimental attachment to a comfortable setting when it is quietly endangering the bhakti of those you are responsible for.
    Analogy

    When termites enter the granary, the wise farmer does not negotiate with them — he moves the grain. Upananda counsels that Gokula be left because the place itself has become a stage for assassins of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; protecting bhakti means relocating from the spot the asuras target, not arguing them out of it. Daya for the community is sometimes departure.

    Stories
    The Pāṇḍavas' wanderings

    Through the Mahābhārata, Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers repeatedly relocate when a place becomes hostile to their dharma — leaving Hastināpura for Vāraṇāvata, leaving Vāraṇāvata after the lac-house, leaving the forest for thirteen years, leaving even Virāṭa's court when their incognito ended. The pattern: protect the dharma-bearing souls; the place can be replaced.

    In Gauḍīya tradition, the Six Gosvāmīs left Bengal and Orissa to settle in Vraja under Caitanya's instruction. Place-shift in service of bhakti is part of the sampradāya's DNA. Upananda's counsel in this verse is the first such relocation in Kṛṣṇa's own līlā — the seed of the principle.

    Important Words
    • muktaḥ — was delivered
      Past passive participle of muc (to release). The same root as mukti. The verse uses ordinary survival (escape from Pūtanā) but the word carries soteriological weight — every escape from death is a small mokṣa-event traceable to Hari's hand.
    • rākṣasyāḥ — from the Rākṣasī (Pūtanā)
      Genitive feminine — 'from the demoness's grasp.' Pūtanā is a paradigmatic Bhāgavatam-figure: the destroyer of infants. Gauḍīya commentators emphasize that despite her demoniac intent, the form of her act (offering her breast) earned her a destination higher than many sages — bhakta-vaśya cuts strangely deep.
    • hareḥ anugrahāt — by the mercy of Hari
      Anugraha — favor, grace. From anu-grah (to grasp on behalf of). The Gauḍīya teaching: Hari literally 'grasps' the soul anu — alongside, supporting. The phrase is the doctrinal hinge of the verse: not luck (daiva), not fortune (bhāgya), but specifically Hari's anugraha.
    • anaḥ ca — and the handcart
      Anas — handcart. The Śakaṭāsura episode (SB 10.7), where a demon possessed the cart and tried to crush the infant Kṛṣṇa, who shattered it with His foot. The verse compresses the entire episode into a single conjunction, trusting the listener to fill in the rest from the family's shared rasa-memory.
    The child Kṛṣṇa, simply by the mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, was somehow or other rescued from the hands of the Rākṣasī Pūtanā, who was determined to kill Him. Then, again by the mercy of the Supreme Godhead, the handcart missed falling upon the child.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The child Kṛṣṇa, simply by the mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, was somehow or other rescued from the hands of the Rākṣasī Pūtanā, who was determined to kill Him. Then, again by the mercy of the Supreme Godhead, the handcart missed falling upon the child.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    By mentioning Rākṣasas, Upananda hints that it is impossible for the people to counteract them. What to speak of children counteracting them. Somehow Kṛṣṇa was saved. We did not directly see the cause. By some inconceivable cause he was saved. The word hi that it was well know, experienced by all the people. He then explains the cause of Kṛṣṇa’s safety. It was because of the mercy of the Lord certainly (nūnam) (though we could not see it directly).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The great dangers are described. By themselves they could not prevent these disasters. This is described in three verses. Since Kṛṣṇa was an infant (bālakaḥ) he could not by himself free himself. We did not directly see the cause. By some inconceivable fortune he was saved. He is our very life (asau). The word hi that the elders (gopa-vṛddhāḥ verse 21) had experienced this. That meeting was suitable for the elders. The youngsters were not present. Or asau indicates that Upananda brought him to the assembly so all could directly see him. Or Kṛṣṇa came there by himself out of curiosity. Nūnam indicates certainty. By the mercy of the Lord who removes all miseries and disasters (hareḥ) from him, he was saved from the cart. He escaped from the Rākṣaṣī, who could do nothing against the protection mantras of Yaśodā and others, while in the house of us devotees. That is our good fortune. When the cart fell on him while he was sleeping under it far off in a lonely place, the cart broke. By the mercy of the Lord, that miracle happened.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa's escape from Pūtanā and the cart shows that protection from death comes from Hari's anugraha alone — not our cleverness.
    Practical Applications
    • Before any 'safe' commute or routine task today, pause and acknowledge that the absence of disaster is Kṛṣṇa's anugraha, not luck or your skill.
    • Name one near-miss from your past — illness, accident, ruined plan — and offer fresh gratitude to Kṛṣṇa for the rescue you did not author.
    • Refuse the modern reflex to credit 'safety systems' or your own foresight; speak aloud at least once today, 'harer anugrahāt — by His mercy.'
    Analogy

    A child wanders the edge of a cliff and arrives home unharmed, and the parent knows that no fence and no luck explains the survival — only the unseen hand that held the child away from the edge. Pūtanā, the cart, every threat: Kṛṣṇa's escape is by Hari's anugraha, not by clever fortune. Survival itself is mercy, accounted to no other cause.

    Stories
    Dhruva protected in the forest

    When five-year-old Dhruva left the palace to perform tapasyā in the wild forests, he ought to have been killed many times over — by beasts, hunger, cold, demons. He was not, because Bhagavān's anugraha shielded him invisibly until he came to his realization (SB 4.8–9).

    Gauḍīya tradition reads such episodes as a single repeated teaching: the survival of the devotee is never to be credited to luck, fortune, or even to the devotee's own vigilance. It is hareḥ anugrahāt — by the mercy of Hari. Upananda is invoking this exact theology in his council speech to justify the move from Gokula.

    Important Words
    • cakra - vātena — by the whirlwind-demon
      Cakra-vāta — circling wind, the meteorological form Tṛṇāvarta took. The instrumental marks the means: even when an asura attacks, he must take a natural form to do so. Gauḍīya teaching: demons in līlā are always 'natural causes' to the unawakened — the devotee learns to see the daitya behind the wind.
    • daityena — by the demon
      Daitya — a son of Diti; the standard category of asura in śāstra. The verse moves from the natural cause (whirlwind) to the personal cause (daitya) — the same movement of seeing the Gauḍīya commentators want the reader to make in his own life.
    • śilāyām — on a slab of stone
      Śilā — rock, stone. The stone on which Tṛṇāvarta crashes echoes Govardhana — the stone Kṛṣṇa would later lift — and śālagrāma-śilā, the worshipable form of Viṣṇu. Stone in the Bhāgavatam is rarely accidental: it carries the weight of Bhagavān's stability.
    • paritrātaḥ — was saved
      Pari-trā — to protect all around. The 'pari' intensifies: protection on every side, not just from one direction. Gauḍīya teaching: when Hari's rakṣaṇa works, it is total — the devotee is held safe in every dimension simultaneously.
    • sura - īśvaraiḥ — by the lords of the gods (Viṣṇu and associates)
      Sureśvara — usually 'the lord of the gods' (Viṣṇu) or 'the chiefs among the gods.' Gauḍīya commentators read it as Viṣṇu Himself with His pārṣadas (eternal associates). Even Kṛṣṇa's līlā-protection in Vraja moves through this Vaikuṇṭha-channel.
    Then again, the demon Tṛṇāvarta, in the form of a whirlwind, took the child away into the dangerous sky to kill Him, but the demon fell down onto a slab of stone. In that case also, by the mercy of Lord Viṣṇu or His associates, the child was saved.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Then again, the demon Tṛṇāvarta, in the form of a whirlwind, took the child away into the dangerous sky to kill Him, but the demon fell down onto a slab of stone. In that case also, by the mercy of Lord Viṣṇu or His associates, the child was saved.
    Commentary

    Asau refers to krsna.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He was taken by the demon into the sky, full of danger, since it was high, without any support (vi—padam—without a base). He was saved by associates sent by the Lord. The word api in the next verse indicates that in this case also the Lord (along with his associates) saved him.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Ayam indicates that the event happened soon after, or concerning the same person. Or it indicates affection, by showing the inauspicious act of Tṛnāvarta. He was taken by the demon into the sky, full of danger, since it was high, without any support (vi—padam—without a base). Or he took him in the sky which was dangerous (vipadam) because if he fell he would be killed. Though it is not suitable to speak of the Lord in this manner, it was done to invoke a sense of fear. Or it is stated out of anxiety arising from great affection according to aniṣṭāśaṅkīnī bandhu-hṛdayāni bhavanti: a relative or intimate friend is always fearful of some injury to his beloved. (Abhijṣāna-śakuntalā-nāṭaka) This should be understood in later statements like na mriyeta (verse 26). Though he fell, he fell on stone. Above and below there was danger. He was saved by the best devatās (sureśvaraiḥ). Or thinking of the great power of the Lord to protect in all circumstances, out of respect the Supreme Lord is indicated by using the plural (sureśvaraiḥ).

    Personal Guidance
    Even when overwhelming forces seize you, Kṛṣṇa's rakṣaṇa is silently at work — the demon falls, the child is saved.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one 'whirlwind' currently lifting you off the ground — a deadline, a craving, a fear — and consciously place it in Kṛṣṇa's hands before acting on it today.
    • When a situation feels beyond your control, refuse the impulse to grip harder; instead, chant one round of japa and let the daityena exhaust itself against the śilā of His protection.
    • Speak Kṛṣṇa's name aloud once today in a moment of ordinary safety, acknowledging that the unremarkable survival of this hour is itself sureśvarair paritrāṇa.
    Analogy

    A great wind lifts a child off His feet and seems to carry Him into nothingness — and then the wind itself shatters, and the child stands on stone, unharmed. Whatever appears to seize Kṛṣṇa's devotee is silently undone by His associates; the daitya exhausts itself against the śilā of His protection, and the child remains.

    Stories
    Tṛṇāvarta's whirlwind

    Tṛṇāvarta, sent by Kaṁsa as a whirlwind-demon, lifted the infant Kṛṣṇa into the dust-darkened sky. The Vrajavāsīs lost sight of Him; Yaśodā fainted. But Kṛṣṇa, grasping the demon's throat, made Himself unbearably heavy until Tṛṇāvarta crashed onto a slab of stone and died, while the child was found unharmed (SB 10.7.20–32).

    Gauḍīya commentators emphasize the verse's phrase 'sureśvarair paritrātaḥ' — saved by the lords of the gods (i.e. by Viṣṇu and His associates). Even when Bhagavān Himself is the protected, the protection is staged through His own personal energies, dramatizing the doctrine that all rakṣaṇa originates in Viṣṇu and flows through His associates.

    • drumayoḥ antaram — the space between the two trees
      Antara — interval, space. The locative situates the children precisely in the danger-zone: between the trees, in the path of their fall. The grammatical precision is the doctrinal point — they were not 'near' but 'between,' and yet untouched.
    • bālakaḥ asau — that child (Kṛṣṇa)
      The demonstrative 'asau' (that one) marks Kṛṣṇa specifically. Gauḍīya commentators: Upananda's rhetoric refers to Kṛṣṇa as 'that child' as if from the outside, because he does not yet know — fully — what the council will later guess: that the child is svayaṁ-bhagavān, and the rakṣaṇa is His own self-protection.
    • tat api acyuta - rakṣaṇam — in that case also, protection by the infallible
      Acyuta-rakṣaṇa — the precise Gauḍīya phrase. Rakṣaṇa (protection) by Acyuta (the never-falling). The phrase explicitly names the agent: not luck, not the boys' nimbleness, but Acyuta Himself. The verse closes Upananda's argument with this doctrinal anchor.
    Even the other day, neither Kṛṣṇa nor any of His playmates died from the falling of the two trees, although the children were near the trees or even between them. This also is to be considered the mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Even the other day, neither Kṛṣṇa nor any of His playmates died from the falling of the two trees, although the children were near the trees or even between them. This also is to be considered the mercy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He speaks with choked voice and tears. He uses incomplete language out of grief. Another version has tatrāpi instead of tad api.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though it was improper to speak of death, he does so to have everyone recollect the inauspiciousness of the event in order to increase everyone’s affection for Kṛṣṇa. He was protected by the Lord who spreads everywhere without fail (acyuta). It would be impossible for anyone else to protect the boys who were scattered all over from the falling of the tall trees.

    When the twin arjuna trees fell and no child was hurt, Kṛṣṇa's silent rakṣaṇa was already at work — His protection precedes our awareness of danger.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice three near-misses from today or this week and name each one aloud as acyuta-rakṣaṇam rather than luck.
    • Before any risky task — driving, a hard conversation, a child's outing — pause and explicitly place it under Kṛṣṇa's shelter instead of relying on your own vigilance.
    • Refuse to take credit for a safe outcome today; tell one person that the protection came from Kṛṣṇa, not from your competence.
    Analogy

    Two great pillars fall on either side of a child playing on the floor, and the child plays on — every dust-motion of the falling stones evaded by an invisible hand. The yamala-arjunas crash and no boy is hurt, because acyuta-rakṣaṇam was already in place before the danger declared itself.

    Stories
    Gajendra at the river-edge

    When the elephant-king Gajendra was seized by the crocodile and had exhausted his own strength, he cried out and Bhagavān appeared instantly — not a moment after the rescue would have failed, but in the perfect window of need (SB 8.2–3). Gauḍīya commentators emphasize that Hari's rakṣaṇa precedes the devotee's awareness of need; the cry only completes the contract.

    The present verse's 'tat api acyuta-rakṣaṇam' is the same teaching in Vraja key. Even before the boys knew they were in danger, the protection was already in place. The trees fell; the boys did not die. The rakṣaṇa is silent and prior; the devotee's task is to recognize it after the fact and offer thanks.

    Important Words
    • autpātikaḥ — disturbance-causing
      Derived from utpāta — the same word repeated through the chapter. Here grammatically the agent is named: an autpātika (a calamity-causing one). Gauḍīya teaching: the same word that started as ambiguous portent in verse 3 has resolved by verse 27 into a named, agent-bearing threat. Discernment has matured.
    • ariṣṭaḥ — the demon (foe)
      Ariṣṭa — literally 'unharmed,' euphemistically the demon (because his name negates auspiciousness). Gauḍīya commentators identify this as a generic reference to the asura agent behind the disturbances — likely Kaṁsa working through his minions, though the verse leaves it general.
    • vrajam — this Vrajabhūmi
      Accusative — 'against Vraja.' The threat is now framed as a threat to Vraja as a whole, not just to the children. Gauḍīya theology: an attack on any element of the Vraja-mandala is an attack on Kṛṣṇa's sva-jana; the protection-decision involves the whole rasa-environment.
    • bālān upādāya — taking the boys with us
      Upādāya — having taken up. The infinitive of action: pick them up, bring them along. Gauḍīya teaching: real relocation is not abandonment — it is the carrying of the protected to safety. The dependents come with the move; nothing precious is left behind.
    • sa - anugāḥ — with our followers
      Sa-anuga — with retinue. Gauḍīya teaching: sādhana is a saṅga-event, not solitary. When the community moves, it moves whole — with its servants, juniors, animals, and elders. The integrity of the saṅga is the integrity of the sādhana.
    All these incidents are being caused by some unknown demon. Before he comes here to create another disturbance, it is our duty to go somewhere else with the boys until there are no more disturbances.
    Purport

    Upananda suggested, “By the mercy of Lord Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa has always been saved from so many dangerous incidents. Now let us leave this place and go someplace where we may worship Lord Viṣṇu undisturbed, before there is another cause of death from some demon who may attack us.” A devotee desires only that he may execute devotional service undisturbed. Actually we see, however, that even during the presence of Kṛṣṇa, when Nanda Mahārāja and the other cowherd men had the Supreme Personality of Godhead in their presence, there were disturbances. Of course, in every case, Kṛṣṇa came out victorious. The instruction we may derive from this is that we should not be disturbed by so-called disturbances. There have been so many disturbances to our Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, but we cannot give up our forward march. On the contrary, people are receiving this movement very enthusiastically all over the world, and they are purchasing literature about Kṛṣṇa consciousness with redoubled energy. Thus there are both encouragements and disturbances. This was so even in Kṛṣṇa’s time.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    All these incidents are being caused by some unknown demon. Before he comes here to create another disturbance, it is our duty to go somewhere else with the boys until there are no more disturbances.
    Commentary

    "Previously in this village there was so much kirtana, worship and darsana of Visnu. Since Nanda’s son was born, everywhere at every moment the kirtana and darsana has been only about Visnu. Now, where should we worship Visnu so that he will always protect us? We should follow the niti sastra given by Visnu."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He has been protected many times by the Lord. What worship we must have performed so that the Lord does this for us! According the scriptures concerning proper conduct (nīti-śāstra) which are sponsored by the Lord, we should immediately leave this dangerous place. So that misfortune arising from disturbances (autpātikaḥ) does not afflict the people of Vraja (meaning Kṛṣṇa), we should go elsewhere, taking the children (meaning Kṛṣṇa).

      His Grace Padaseva Prabhu· Oriya
    Personal Guidance
    When the world threatens our bhakti, the devotee's instinct is not to fight but to relocate — protect the sādhana, protect the children, keep moving toward Kṛṣṇa.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one environment (a chat, a feed, a room) that keeps disturbing your sādhana, and physically remove yourself from it today.
    • Refuse to wait for the next 'demon' — proactively rearrange tomorrow's schedule to shield your japa and study time before disturbance strikes.
    • Speak to one person under your care (child, junior, dependent) and make one concrete move today to protect their Kṛṣṇa-conscious atmosphere, not just their bodily comfort.
    Analogy

    When wolves have learned the path to the fold, the shepherd does not station more dogs — he moves the fold. Bhakti's instinct in a recurring threat is not to fortify but to relocate; protect the sādhakas first, the spot second. Upananda counsels going elsewhere, sa-anugāḥ — with all the dependents, so that the bhakti-environment travels intact.

    Stories
    Haridāsa Ṭhākura's relocation

    When Haridāsa Ṭhākura's Kṛṣṇa-conscious life became impossible in his home village (he was beaten on twenty-two market-places for chanting), he relocated to a remote cave and continued his 300,000-name daily japa undisturbed. Caitanya Mahāprabhu later honored him as nāmācārya — the very name-teacher of the sampradāya.

    Gauḍīya tradition: when a place is actively hostile to bhakti, the wise response is not to wait for it to change but to relocate the sādhana to soil that will hold it. Upananda's counsel here is the household-scale of Haridāsa's solitary one — same principle, same wisdom.
